title: Not even empty deceit
source_text: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Παῦλος συνιδὼν ὅτι ἔστιν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ Ἑλληνικῇ οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητα τοῖς πολλοῖς πιθανὰ, παριστάντα τὸ ψεῦδος ὡς ἀλήθειαν, φησὶν ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνοις τό· „βλέπετε, μή τις ὑμᾶς ἔσται ὁ συλαγωγῶν διὰ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου καὶ οὐ κατὰ Χριστόν.“ καὶ ὁρῶν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τῆς τοῦ κόσμου σοφίας ἐμφαινόμενόν τι μέγεθος, εἶπεν εἶναι τοὺς λόγους τῶν φιλοσόφων „κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου.“ οὐδεὶς δὲ τῶν νοῦν ἐχόντων φήσαι ἂν καὶ τὰ Κέλσου „κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου“ εἶναι γεγραμμένα. κἀκεῖνα μὲν ἔχοντά τι ἀπατηλὸν καὶ κενὴν ἀπάτην ὠνόμασε, τάχα πρὸς ἀντιδιαστολὴν ἀπάτης τινὸς οὐ κενῆς. ἣν θεωρήσας ὁ Ἱερεμίας ἐτόλμησε πρὸς θεὸν εἰπεῖν τό· „ἠπάτησάς με, κύριε, καὶ ἠπατήθην, ἐκράτησας καὶ ἠδυνήθης·“ τὰ δὲ Κέλσου οὐδαμῶς ἀπάτην ἔχειν μοι φαίνεται, διὸ οὐδὲ κενὴν, ὁποίαν ἔχει τὰ τῶν αἱρέσεις ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ πηξάντων καὶ τῶν νοῦν οὐ τὸν τυχόντα κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνα ἀνειληφότων. καὶ ὥσπερ οὐ τὸ τυχὸν τῶν ψευδομένων ἐν γεωμετρικοῖς θεωρήμασι ψευδογραφούμενόν τις ἂν λέγοι ἢ καὶ ἀναγράφοι γυμνασίου ἕνεκεν τοῦ ἀπὸ τοιούτων, οὕτως παραπλήσια εἶναι χρὴ τοῖς τῶν αἱρέσεις πηξάντων ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ νοήμασι τὰ μέλλοντα ὁμοίως ἐκείνοις λέγεσθαι κενὴν ἀπάτην καὶ „παράδοσιν ἀνθρώπων, κατὰ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου.“
pass_a_gloss: Paul, then, having perceived (συνοράω) that there are in Greek (Ἑλληνικός) philosophy persuasive things (πιθανά) not easily despised (εὐκαταφρόνητος) by the many, presenting (παρίστημι) falsehood (ψεῦδος) as truth, says regarding them: [Col 2:8: see (βλέπω) lest anyone will be the one carrying you off as spoil (συλαγωγέω) through philosophy and empty (κενός) deceit (ἀπάτη) according to the tradition (παράδοσις) of men, according to the elements (στοιχεῖα) of the world (κόσμος) and not according to Christ]. And seeing some greatness (μέγεθος) appearing (ἐμφαίνω) in the words of the wisdom (σοφία) of the world, he said the words of the philosophers are 'according to the elements of the world'. But no one of those having sense (νοῦς) would say that Celsus's things too are written 'according to the elements of the world'. And those, as having something deceptive (ἀπατηλός), he also named 'empty deceit', perhaps for contradistinction (ἀντιδιαστολή) from some deceit not empty; which Jeremiah having beheld (θεωρέω) dared (τολμάω) to say to God: [Jer 20:7 LXX: you deceived (ἀπατάω) me, Lord, and I was deceived; you prevailed (κρατέω) and were able (δύναμαι)]. But Celsus's things seem to me in no way to have deceit, wherefore not even empty [deceit], such as the things of those who fixed/founded (πήγνυμι) schools (αἱρέσεις) in philosophy have, and of those who took up (ἀναλαμβάνω) no ordinary (οὐ τὸν τυχόντα) mind in those things. And just as one would not call any chance one (τὸ τυχόν) of the falsehoods in geometrical theorems (γεωμετρικὰ θεωρήματα) a false diagram/fallacious proof (ψευδογραφέω, pass. ptc.), or even record (ἀναγράφω) it for the sake of the exercise (γυμνάσιον) from such things, so the things that are to be called, like those, empty deceit and 'tradition of men, according to the elements of the world' must be close (παραπλήσιος) to the thoughts (νοήματα) of those who founded schools in philosophy.
pass_b_english: Paul, then, saw that Greek philosophy holds persuasive arguments, not easy for most people to dismiss, which present falsehood as truth. Of these he says: “See to it that no one carries you off as spoil through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). And seeing that a certain greatness shows itself in the words of the wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 1:20), he said that the words of the philosophers were “according to the elements of the world.” But no one with any sense would say that Celsus’s writings too were written “according to the elements of the world.”

Those words of the philosophers, since they hold something deceptive, he also called “empty deceit” (Colossians 2:8), perhaps to distinguish it from a deceit that is not empty. Jeremiah perceived this other deceit and dared to say to God: “You deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you were stronger, and you prevailed” (Jeremiah 20:7). But Celsus’s writings seem to me to hold no deceit at all, and therefore not even empty deceit, such as is found in the writings of those who founded schools in philosophy and who gained no ordinary understanding in those matters.

Just as no one would call any chance error in geometrical theorems a fallacious proof, or write it up as an exercise for training in such matters, so whatever is to be called, like those words of the philosophers, “empty deceit” and “the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world” (Colossians 2:8), must come close to the thoughts of those who founded schools in philosophy.

choices.choice: Jeremiah 20:7 has the same chapter and verse in the LXX and the English Bible; Origen's LXX ends 'ἐκράτησας καὶ ἠδυνήθης' (you prevailed and were able); 'you were stronger, and you prevailed' renders the pair (κρατέω = be strong, master; δύναμαι = be able, prevail) without adding an object the Greek lacks. 'τῆς τοῦ κόσμου σοφίας' (the wisdom of the world) is Paul's own phrase (1 Corinthians 1:20, τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου; compare 3:19), used here of Paul's view, so it is cited inline as a clear allusion. 'αἱρέσεις ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ πηξάντων' = those who founded philosophical schools (αἵρεσις here in its neutral classical sense, not 'heresy'). 'ψευδογραφούμενον' is the technical term (as in Aristotle) for a fallacious geometrical proof, which errs while working from the proper principles of geometry, as against a merely random mistake; rendered 'fallacious proof'. The comparison says that Celsus's errors are of the random kind, not the kind worth studying. 'μή τις ὑμᾶς ἔσται ὁ συλαγωγῶν' rendered 'that no one carries you off as spoil' (συλαγωγέω, to carry off as plunder).

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.

changes: 'that the many cannot lightly dismiss, which make falsehood look like truth' -> 'not easy for most people to dismiss, which present falsehood as truth' (οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητα: 'not easily despised', not 'cannot'; παριστάντα = present)
Added (1 Corinthians 1:20) for 'the wisdom of the world', Paul's own phrase used of Paul
Added (Colossians 2:8) to the later quotations of 'empty deceit' and 'the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world' in paragraphs 2 and 3
'he called' -> 'he also called' (καὶ κενὴν ἀπάτην ὠνόμασε); 'beheld' -> 'perceived' (θεωρήσας)
'brought no ordinary intelligence' -> 'gained no ordinary understanding' (νοῦν ... ἀνειληφότων = acquired)

Restored the 'just as ... so' frame (ὥσπερ ... οὕτως) that had been split into two sentences; 'like the teachings of the philosophers' -> 'like those words of the philosophers' (ὁμοίως ἐκείνοις refers back to κἀκεῖνα)
Checked Jeremiah 20:7: same number in LXX and English; Origen's wording 'ἐκράτησας καὶ ἠδυνήθης' matches the rendering; Colossians 2:8 matches
